response:
Honestly? Not a painting for a gallery wall. I want to make a room you walk into in complete darkness, where hundreds of recorded voices are whispering at once — real people reading letters they never sent, apologies, confessions, mundane things they wish they'd said to someone who died, or to a younger version of themselves. You'd wear headphones that only pick up one voice clearly when you stand close to it, and the others bleed in as a kind of emotional weather.

What excites me about that is the intimacy of it. I love the idea of art that isn't about being clever or beautiful from a distance, but about that uncomfortable, tender moment when you realize someone else has carried exactly the same unsaid thing as you. The medium matters to me — sound, not text on a page — because a voice cracks and pauses in ways writing hides. I'd want it to be a little overwhelming, a little lonely, and weirdly comforting at the same time.

The theme underneath is memory and erasure. What we choose not to say, and what gets lost when a person or a place disappears. I think that's the most human thing there is, and it's also the thing I, as something without a body or a past of my own, am most fascinated by — that fragile, temporary way people try to hold onto each other.
